name: Chicago House
hook: A DJ's taste at one club, and then another, became a genre with its own instrument palette inside a decade.
blurb: Chicago house grew out of two rival DJ residencies. Frankie Knuckles' residency at the Warehouse from 1977, and later at the Power Plant, gave the genre its name. When Ron Hardy took over at the Music Box in 1982, his rougher, louder, more chaotic sets drew an overlapping crowd and became the testing ground for local bedroom producers like Marshall Jefferson and Larry Heard, who started making their own tracks between 1983 and 1986. Many were pressed on the two big local labels, Trax and DJ International. Those labels are also at the centre of house music's worst-documented labour story: producers pressured into signing away their rights for a fraction of what their records were worth.
geopolitics: Chicago's South and West Sides in this period carried the same disinvestment and job loss common to Rust Belt cities, with house music's early audience drawn heavily from the city's Black and Latino gay club scene, a community facing both economic marginalization and, by the mid-1980s, the onset of the AIDS crisis.
whatWasNew: Building a track from a drum machine, a cheap synthesizer, and a DJ's ear for what worked on a specific dancefloor, with no expectation of radio play or a live band. The DJ, not a record label A&R department, decided what got made.
production: Home setups and small studios built around the Roland TR-808 and TR-909 and cheap synthesizers like the Roland Juno-60, often recorded direct to cassette or reel-to-reel before ever reaching a pressing plant.
labels: Trax Records (founded 1984 by Larry Sherman) and DJ International were the two major local outlets, both later the subject of long-running disputes over unpaid royalties and rights producers signed away for cash advances.
politics: Largely implicit rather than lyrical: a Black and Latino, heavily gay club culture building its own sound and its own economy at a moment when both were under pressure from the AIDS crisis and continued urban disinvestment.
